results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 63 non-callout outline units align one-to-one, in order, with the spec paragraphs p01-p63 (including the declared order p14 before p12, p39 inside Team Shapes, p49 after Team Shapes), and each summary states the aligned controlling idea: e.g. Owning ¶1 "Defining system of record and integration contract" = p14; Teams ¶8 "journey teams plus an integration pair, with its limit" = p24; Stages ¶1 "Change team shape one stage before the system landscape" = p49; Conclusion ¶1 "the map gives the lost order an owner" = p58. The three callouts match no spec paragraph (null).

results.draft_locus: Team Shapes for a Commerce Merchant ¶12
results.quote: A shared standard is one half of the lesson. Werner Vogels' 2006 line "you build it, you run it", relayed by AWS's blog at the time, is the other half: the team that changes a flow is the team paged when it fails.
results.finding: The outliner needed two phrases ("Journey teams need a shared integration standard; and the team that changes a flow is paged for it"). The spec's idea is one lesson drawn from the two cautions; the draft derives the shared standard from them but attaches the Vogels line as an asserted "other half" without tying it to Uber's caution (ownership spread so wide that a failure is slow to trace), so it reads as a second, unrelated rule. Both flow readers stumbled on this sentence. Tie the second half to Uber: the team that changes a flow is paged, so a failure is traced by one team.

results.draft_locus: Working With Agencies and Implementation Partners ¶1
results.quote: Such evidence says little about who owns the result after launch, which is the gap the rules below close. The vendor-side mechanisms for agency work are structural
results.finding: The outliner needed two phrases ("Agency-built evidence (Hobbycraft) is silent on post-launch ownership; and vendor mechanisms for partner builds"). The paragraph reaches its point (the evidence is silent on ownership, which the rules close) and then opens a new topic, the vendors' mechanisms for agency builds, after it. Order the paragraph around its one idea (agencies build; vendors and evidence alike are set up for build-and-transfer, not for owning after launch) and end on the gap the rules close.

Engineering Practices ¶8 (p47), marked two_ideas (METR trial; Shopify mandate): the draft joins them with "Adoption is being pushed whatever the measurements say", so the paragraph has one idea (measured results and the push to adopt diverge), as the spec declares. No other unit was marked.

Every unit traces to a supporting claim: introduction to the thesis; scene and owning to S1/S2; map to S2; team shapes to S3 (PM paragraph to S5); stages to S6/S3; agencies and vendors to S4; governance and practices (incl. AI tools, framed as changing how fast stock/price code reaches production) to S5; In Practice to S2-S4; When It Goes Wrong to S1/S2/S4; conclusion synthesizes S1-S6. Hobbycraft (p28) and the Uber caution (p26) trace only weakly; their problems are recorded under flow and one-idea results.

results.quote: | Integrations | 34 | 14 (flows in the iPaaS, the integration team under Ruben Alves) | 9 (scripts, mostly from 2019–2022) |

It counts 9 integrations as "Owned by the agency" although the chapter's rule (and Figure 2, "the agency as a contributor rather than an owner") says every row needs an owner inside the company; and the bol stock script, a 2021 agency script, is among the 5 with "No named owner", so the reader cannot tell which bucket agency scripts fall into. State in the text what the agency column means (agency-maintained, internal owner still to be named, or the like) and why the bol script is counted as unowned, and keep installers out of the owner column.

The introduction opens on a puzzling scenario (an order lost between three suppliers each reporting its part working), states the problem and the chapter's question, places the setting, gives the thesis and a roadmap with evidence. None of placeholder, restated question, dictionary, "dawn of man" or book report.

The conclusion opens with the callback rather than "in conclusion", sorts findings into established / depends on context / the author's synthesis, adds diagnostic questions and a hand-off. It restates evidence briefly but introduces no new idea or subtopic and is not a grab bag or bare thesis restatement.

p58 states what no single section states: team shape, contracts, vendor card and governance all exist to keep the map's rows filled, and the lost order is traced by an owner with a row, a monitor and a calendar; the three incidents were failures of ownership. The so-what is given in p61 (the map is the first artifact and the only one that prevents incidents on its own; change team shape one stage ahead) and the nine questions turn it into action.

p58 opens: "The opening's order that reached checkout but never the warehouse, while each supplier reported its own part working, is the case the map is built for" and says who traces it with the map in place, as callback.to declares.

The intro reader predicted the topic (an internal technical owner per system, integration and app who decides, changes, watches, fixes and retires), the reason (ownership follows how agencies and vendors are paid), the setting (a merchant with about a dozen engineers, an agency and several vendors), journey teams plus an integration pair, light governance of facts, the full section order as in the roadmap, the evidence (Kestrel & Pine's map and incidents, a platform's partner payments, Conway, Team Topologies, Zalando and Uber, decision records, dated AI studies) and the tone. It did not restate the opening lost-order hook, but its answer carries the substance the hook argues (flows between suppliers need an owner inside the merchant).

The reader names the missing owner (no row, no internal technical owner with the five duties), the money reason (agency paid to build, not to own), the unpinned version and uncalendared retirement date, the missing stock-sync monitor, and the prevention: a map row with internal owner, pinned version and "watched by" monitor, the vendor card's deprecation calendar, the standing pinning rule, the architecture hour's ninety-day deprecation review, and a statement of work naming versions with a deprecation clause; it explicitly calls it a published change meeting an unowned dependency, not bad code. It does not name the integration pair as the owner, a minor omission.

The reader says a team per vendor copies every integration gap into the organization chart, makes handoffs between systems handoffs between people, leaves nobody owning the journey (the Spaghetti Junction in the org chart), and replaces it with one or two stream-aligned journey teams (buy; fulfill and return, with their contents), an integration pair owning the integration layer, map and reconciliation as an internal product, a small data function, vendors and agency under written contracts, a shared integration standard, and one journey team plus one integration engineer below eight. Conway is not named and the reason for a pair rather than a team (bottleneck) is missing, but the substance is there.

The reader lists every expected term: merchant owns repository, vendor accounts, credentials, map and decision records with the agency committing to the merchant's repository; every deliverable a map row with scopes, pinned version, tested release and exit plan; statement of work naming versions and a deprecation clause; post-launch ownership agreed in writing before launch (agency with a named engineer or the merchant); building separated from keeping; and Kestrel & Pine's 2027 statement of work with nine scripts, owners and pinned versions, three moved in-house.
